newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico port closures delay, don't sink oil exports.
newsitem.headline: Mexico port closures delay, don't sink oil exports.

text.p: Weekly openings and closings of Mexico's Gulf of Mexico crude oil ports cause shipment delays and jitters in world oil markets, but state oil monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) chief Adrian Lajous said it no has definitive impact on the country's exports.
"The openings and closings of ports have no affect on export activity... and represent no basic obstacle to our export program," Lajous said at a recent press conference.
"There is usually a certain time of year when the ports close and open because of winds from the north," he added.

"Of course the closures affect activity at the ports and can cause delays of a couple days. It's normal for about six months of the year," a local shipping company director, who declined to be named, said.
Although he said Mother Nature can not be controlled, he suggested the government plan around and better predict poor weather.

Strides toward improved port communication have been made this year, as the government said it outfitted its ports with improved,24-hour radar technology last month. "As exports rise we will have to strengthen port infrastructure," Lajous said.

Since October, Mexico's three main oil ports -- Cayo Arcas, Dos Bocas and Pajaritos -- have been open and shut about once a week, and occasionally for a few days at a time. The closures prevent ships from sailing from the ports and disrupt export timetables.
Pemex officials have said delayed shipments when ports are shut are sent out in the days after the port reopens in a almost constant rescheduling of the national crude fleet.
While sources in Mexico's shipping industry have said the closures this winter season have been similar to past years, they acknowledge export and import delays are a problem.
Yet some crude ports close more often than others, acting on different shipping policies.

Pajaritos in Veracruz and Dos Bocas in Tabasco tend to shut down when winds reach 50 kilometers per hour (30 miles per hour), or when wave heights are considered dangerous. At times, these ports close on anticipation of bad weather, port officials said.
In contrast, at Pemex's third and largest port, Cayo Arcas in Campeche state, the terminal rarely closes to crude shipments, even when surrounding ports shut.
"The weather has to be pretty bad for us to close for crude operations," Cayo Arcas port Capt. Jorge Luis Rios MacBeth told Reuters.
He said the port does not close in anticipation of poor shipping conditions, but only when Pemex determines the crude tankers are deemed unable to sail.

Cayo Arcas ships about 611,000 barrels per day (bpd), Dos Bocas ships and average 440,000 bpd and Pajaritos ships about 399,000 bpd, according to Pemex. Most crude is exported to clients in the United States.
Pemex's crude servicing for the Far East, via Salina Cruz port in Oaxaca state on the Pacific coast, also closes frequently in the winter months because of its location on the Gulf of Tehuantepec.
Pemex officials said closures at the port have little impact on shipments equivalent to 90,000 bpd sent out about once per week to Asian clients.
